messages.author: fecbe3dc811bed89
messages.subject: binary vector, but permuted randomly
parts:
Hi Stan developers,

I have asked same question on JAGS forum (https://sourceforge.net/p/mcmc-jags/discussion/610037/thread/ab8cfeda/), but still didn't get a good solution to this. So I am not sure whether STAN can handle it or not? Thanks!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] binary vector, but permuted randomly
parts:
What do you want to do with the permutation? I ask because it
matters for how or whether you even can do it in Stan (not
all caps).

It's easy in generated quantities (just code Knuth's algorithm),
will be easy in Stan 2.11 in transformed data, but if you want to
do it directly with parameters, it'll depend on what you want to
do with it.

Also, I'm guessing there'll be a better approach to whatever
you want to do than literally permuting an existing array or
vector.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] binary vector, but permuted randomly
parts:
To echo Bob, we can only speculate unless you have an actual
model in mind. For example, if you have a generative model
where a set of items is randomly permuted and then one is
randomly selected then you don’t have to do the permutations at
all — marginalizing over all possible permutations gives you the
uniform distribution over those items.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] binary vector, but permuted randomly

Is there some neat dynamic programming algorithm that makes

It’s analytic — a uniform distribution over permutations of N
items preserves the uniform distribution over those N items.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] binary vector, but permuted randomly
parts:
One of the very important features of Baysian inference is that
it decouples inference from decision making.  A natural Bayesian
fit will not feature cut-offs such as “variable included or not” but
rather try to estimate the importance of each variable.  When
you try to force decision making into an inference problem you
run into no end of trouble, as you are seeing.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] binary vector, but permuted randomly
parts:
Nope, I have nothing to add. I don't know what Bayesian variable
selection is. You mean a discrete mixture with non-zero probabilty
mass at zero? We can't code that in Stan because it's O(2^N)
computational complexity (time and space both for us) with N parameters.
And we probably won't try to code any workarounds within Stan.
Despite Andrew not liking spike-and-slab priors, the paper I
referenced from Aki has that in the title and explains how to do
it as a post-process for time series examples.

- Bob

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] binary vector, but permuted randomly
parts:
I'm not sure I understand why some parameters need to be set to zero, so I apologize if the rest of my comment is irrelevant, but if you're doing full Bayes then I suggest just letting small coefficients be estimated to be small if that's what the model says. Regularization of large estimates has a much bigger impact on the predictive performance of your model than does setting small parameters to zero.

Jonah
